question.text:
We consider a function $f(x)$ defined for all real numbers. We suppose that the first and second derivatives $f^{\prime}(x)$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$ are also defined for all real numbers. Below we show the graph of the second derivative of $f$. You may assume that $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$ is decreasing outside of the region shown.

Suppose that $f^{\prime}(0)=5$. How many critical points does $f$ have?

Suppose $f$ is a function such that $f^{\prime}(x)=4 x^3$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)=12 x^2$.

Which of the following is /are true?

  1. $f$ has a local maximum at $x=0$ by the first derivative test
  2. $f$ has a local minimum at $x=0$ by the first derivative test
  3. $f$ has a local maximum at $x=0$ by the second derivative test
  4. $f$ has a local minimum at $x=0$ by the second derivative test

Which of the following represents the value of $\displaystyle{}\int_1^e \frac{\ln (x)}{x} d x ?$
  1. $1$
  2. $2$
  3. $1 / 2$
  4. $e$

Suppose $h(x)$ is a function such that $h(x)$ has exactly three critical point. Two of which are shown in the table below.
Assume that both $h(x)$ and $h^{\prime}(x)$ are differentiable on $(-\infty, \infty)$
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline x & 0 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\
\hline h(x) & 2 & ? & 4 & 4 \\
\hline h^{\prime}(x) & -1 & 0 & 0 & ? \\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Further using Lagrange mean value theorem in the interval $[5,7],$ we can determine the interval of the third critical point.
On which of the following intervals must $h(x)$ be increasing on the entire interval?

  1. $(0,3)$
  2. $(3,5)$
  3. $(5,6)$
  4. $(6,7)$

Let $q(x)$ be a continuous function which is defined for all real numbers. A portion of the graph of $q^{\prime}(x),$ the derivative of $\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{x}),$ is shown below.

On which of the following interval(s) is $q^{\prime \prime}(x)$ positive?

  1. $(0,2)$
  2. $(2,4)$
  3. $(7,9)$
  4. $(5,7)$

Find $\displaystyle\int x e^{-3 x} d x$

  1. $\dfrac{1}{2} e^{-3 x}(x-3)+C$

     

  2. $-\dfrac{1}{9} e^{-3 x}(3 x+1)+C$

     

  3. $-\dfrac{1}{6} x^2 e^{-3 x}+C$

     

  4. $-\dfrac{1}{3} e^{-3 x}(x+1)+C$

If $g$ is continuous (but not differentiable) at $x=0, g(0)=8$, and $f(x)=x g(x),$ find $f^{\prime}(0)$.

  1. $0$
  2. $8$
  3. $1$
  4. $f(x)$ is also not differentiable at $x=0$.

Is there a number $b$ such that $\displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow-2} \frac{b x^2+15 x+15+b}{x^2+x-2}$ exists? If so, find the value of $b$ and the value of the limit.

  1. $-1$
  2. $-2$
  3. $1$
  4. There is no such $b$ for that above limit exist

The following are tables of values for two differentiable functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ and their derivatives. Missing values are denoted by a $\text{“?"}.$ Assume that each of these functions is defined for all real numbers, that $f^{\prime}(x)$ and $g^{\prime}(x)$ are continuous.
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline x & 0 & 2 & 3 & 6 & 9 \\
\hline f(x) & -1 & ? & 0 & -2 & ? \\
\hline f^{\prime}(x) & 1 & 4 & -1 & ? & 1 \\
\hline
\end{array} \qquad \qquad
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline x & -1 & 1 & 3 & 7 & 11 \\
\hline g(x) & -4 & 1 & 2 & 6 & 7 \\
\hline g^{\prime}(x) & 7 & ? & 3 & 4 & ? \\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Let $z(x)=f(g(x))$. Find $z^{\prime}(3)$
$\displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}(x+\sin x)^{\dfrac{1}{x}}$

Suppose that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are differentiable functions and that $h(x)=f(x) g(x)$. You are given the following table of values:
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline h(1) & 24 \\
\hline g(1) & 6 \\
\hline f^{\prime}(1) & -2 \\
\hline h^{\prime}(1) & 20 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Using the table, find $g^{\prime}(1)$.

The function $f(x)$ is defined as follows:
$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
\dfrac{x}{x^2+1} & x \leq 0 \\
? & x>0
\end{array}\right.
$$
Note that the formula for $f(x)$ for $x>0$ is unknown.

However, it is known that $f(x)$ is differentiable at each point in its domain $(-\infty, \infty)$, and that $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ for all $x \geq 0$.

Which of the following option is/are TRUE?

  1. $x=0$ has global minima
  2. $x=0$ has global maxima
  3. $x=-1$ has global maxima
  4. $x=-1$ has global minima

Let $f$ be a continuous function defined for all real numbers. Suppose
$$
\int_0^3 f(x) d x=2, \quad \int_1^2 f(x) d x=7, \quad \int_3^6 f(x) d x=-5, \quad \text { and } \quad \int_9^{18} f(x) d x=-3
$$
Find $\displaystyle{}\int_3^6 f\left(\frac{1}{3} t\right) d t$

The derivative of $g(x)=e^{\sqrt{x}}$ is

  1. $\sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}-1}$

     

  2. $2 e^{\sqrt{x}} x^{-0.5}$

     

  3. $\dfrac{0.5 e^{\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}$

     

  4. $e^{\sqrt{x}}$
If $f(x)=(1+x)\left(1+x^2\right)\left(1+x^3\right)\left(1+x^4\right),$ then $f^{\prime}(0)=?$

The function $g(x)$ is given by the equation
$$
g(x)= \begin{cases}a x^2 & x \leq 1 \\ b-\ln (3 x) & x>1\end{cases}
$$
where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
Find the value of $a$ such that function is differentiable at $x=1$.

  1. $1 / 2$
  2. $-1 / 2$
  3. $2$
  4. $-2$

Some information about the derivative $p^{\prime}(x)$ and the second derivative $p^{\prime \prime}(x)$ of a function $p(x)$ is provided in the table below.
$$
\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|r|r|}
\hline x & -4 & -3 & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\
\hline p^{\prime}(x) & 1 & 0 & -2 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\
\hline p^{\prime \prime}(x) & -1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
At which of the following values of $x$ must $p(x)$ have a local minimum?
  1. $x=-3$
  2. $x=-2$
  3. $x=-1$
  4. $x=1$

Shown below are portions of the graphs of $y=f(x), y=f^{\prime}(x)$, and $y=f^{\prime \prime}(x)$.
Determine which graph is which.

  1. $A-f(x), B-f^{\prime}(x), C-f^{\prime \prime}(x)$
  2. $A-f^{\prime}(x), B-f(x), C-f^{\prime \prime}(x)$
  3. $A-f^{\prime \prime}(x), B-f(x), C-f^{\prime}(x)$
  4. $A-f^{\prime}(x), B-f^{\prime \prime}(x), C-f(x)$

Which of the following is/are TRUE?

  1. $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^5\left(a x^2+b x+c\right) d x=2 \int_0^5\left(a x^2+c\right) d x$

     

  2. If $f$ and $g$ are continuous and $f(x) \geqslant g(x)$ for $a \leqslant x \leqslant b$, then
    $$
    \int_a^b f(x) d x \geqslant \int_a^b g(x) d x
    $$
  3. If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable, then
    $$
    \frac{d}{d x}[f(g(x))]=f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)
    $$
  4. If $f$ is differentiable, then $\dfrac{d}{d x} \sqrt{f(x)}=\dfrac{f^{\prime}(x)}{2 \sqrt{f(x)}}$.

Suppose $f(x)$ is continuous and diffrentiable for all $x$. And $-1 \leq f^{\prime}(x) \leq 3$ fo all $x$. Which of the following is/are ALWAYS true?

  1. $f(5) \leq f(3)+6$
  2. $f(5) \geq f(3)-2$
  3. $f(5) \leq f(3)+10$
  4. $f(5) \geq f(3)-10$

Below is a portion of the graph of an even function $f(x)$, which has domain $(-\infty, \infty)$ even though the graph below only shows the function on the interval $[0,5]$. Note that $f(x)$ has a vertical asymptote at $x=1$.


Find
$$
\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(1.5+h)-f(1.5)}{h}
$$

Which of the following is/are TRUE?

  1. If $\displaystyle{}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} f(x)=0$ and $\displaystyle{}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} g(x)=0$, then $\displaystyle{}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ does not exist.
  2. If $f, g,$ are any two functions which are continuous for all $x$, then $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is continuous for all $x$.
  3. It is possible that functions $f$ and $g$ are not continuous at a point $x_0,$ but $f+g$ is continuous at $x_0$.
  4. If $f^{\prime}(c)=0$ then $f(x)$ has a local maximum or a local minimum at $x=c$.

Consider the family of functions
$$
g(x)=a \ln (x)+\frac{b}{x}
$$
defined for $x>0,$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

Any function $g(x)$ in this family has only one critical point. In terms of $a$ and $b,$ what is the $x$-coordinate of that critical point?

  1. $x=b / a$ is a critical point where the function shows local minima
  2. $x=b / a$ is a critical point where the function shows local maxima
  3. $x=a / b$ is a critical point where the function shows local minima
  4. $x=a / b$ is a critical point where the function shows local maxima

Consider the piecewise function
$$
q(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
7 e^{x-C}+\dfrac{x}{3 x-2} & \quad x<0 \\ \\
\dfrac{6+5 x}{2+3 x+4^x} & \quad x \geq 0
\end{array}\right.
$$
where $C$ is a constant.
Find $\displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} q(x)$

The function
$$
f(x)= \begin{cases}e^x & \text { if } \quad x \leq 1 \\ m x+b & \text { if } \quad x>1\end{cases}
$$
is continuous and differentiable at $x=1$.

Find the value of $m-b?$

  1. $e$
  2. $-e$
  3. $\mathrm{e}-1$
  4. $1-e$

Find the values of $A$ and $B$ that make
$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
x^2+1 & \text { if } & x \geq 0 \\
A \sin x+B \cos x & \text { if } & x<0
\end{array}\right.
$$
differentiable at $x=0$.

  1. $A=0, B=1$
  2. $A=1, B=0$
  3. $A=0, B=-1$
  4. $A=-1, B=0$

Let $M =  \displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(e^x+3 x\right)^{1 / x}$.

Find the value of $log_eM.$

Consider a continuous function $f(x),$ and suppose that $f(x)$ and its first derivative $f^{\prime}(x)$ are differentiable everywhere. Suppose we know the following information about $f(x)$ and its first and second derivatives.

  • On the interval $(-\infty,-2)$, we have $f(x)=2^{-x}$.
  • $\displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)=6$
  • $f(2)=-5, f(3)=7,$ and $f(4)=8$
  • $f^{\prime}(x)$ is equal to 0 at $x=-1,2,4,$ and not at any other $x$-values.
  • $f^{\prime \prime}(x)<0$ on the intervals $-1<x<0$ and $3<x<5$, and not on any other interval.

Find the global minimum of $f(x)$ on $(-\infty, \infty)?$  (minimum value of $f(x)$)

Define
$$
g(x)= \begin{cases}-6 x+2 & x \leq 2 \\ x-2 & x>2\end{cases}
$$
Find $\displaystyle\int_1^4 g(x) d x$.
